abstract: "Metascientific research has revealed that researchers often fall short in implementing best research practices when designing studies, reporting findings, citing the literature, or sharing data and code. Researchers have time constraints that limit the extent to which they can master all aspects of the research process, and cognitive constraints that limit which practices they remember to implement in their work. By capturing expert knowledge within an automated tool, we aim to elevate the quality of scientific research and disseminate best practices more widely. We illustrate how best practices can be automatically detected by analyzing papers published in Psychological Science in the last decade. Researchers can use the tool before submitting or when reviewing scientific articles. Our module based software tool can easily be extended by experts in the scientific community to automatically check best practices, educate scientists, and increase the quality of scientific reporting."

```{r}
  id = ids,
  filename = filenames,

)

psych_science <- dplyr::left_join(psych_science, works_from_dois[, c("url", "openalex_id", "cited_by_count", "is_retracted", "oa_status")], by = c("url" = "url")
)

# Extract year from the 'issued' column
psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  mutate(year = as.integer(substr(issued, 1, 4)))  # Extract the first 4 characters (year)
```

# Introduction

Metascientific research demonstrates significant room for improvement in how scientists design studies, report findings, and implement open science practices when sharing their work. The uptake of best practices is slow [@sharpe2013resistance], and often suboptimal. For example, researchers often use invalid and unreliable measures [@goos2024assessing], misinterpret non-significant results [@aczel2018quantifying], write insufficiently specific preregistrations [@van2024potential], make mistakes in power analyses [@thibault2024evaluation], and misuse Bayes factors [@tendeiro2024diagnosing]. Although it is the responsibility of scientists to keep up to date on best practices, time constraints and the rapid pace of new developments make this challenging. Peer reviewers, similarly pressed for time, may not identify the absence of best practices. Checklists could potentially increase the adoption of best practices, but in practice they have limited impact, as researchers might not be aware of the existence of checklists, and they still need sufficient expertise to evaluate whether they have adhered to items on the checklist [@dexter2017narrative].

Human factors research suggests that automation (where researchers are kept in the loop) can offer a partial solution. Two recent developments have increased the possibility that best practices can be automatically detected. First, metascientific research has identified where the adoption of best practices is lagging, and offered concrete suggestions for improvement. This work often includes data that can be used as ground truth to validate automated checks. Second, advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence have made it easier to deal with written text, both when turning scientific articles into structured data files (e.g., the GROBID machine learning library), as when extracting or classifying information in written text. This has made it possible to develop algorithms that automatically emulate what experts do when they examine if best practices are present or absent. For example, a reviewer might search for the section in the paper that describes an a-priori power analysis, and then check if people follow best practices, and report the alpha level, desired power, the effect size metric, and a justification for the effect size, for each hypothesis tested [@lakens_justification_2022]. If any of this information is missing, authors should be made aware that they are not following best practices, so that they can improve their paper. While many automated checks for best practices will require only simple text matching based on regular expression, more complex text extraction is possible by using large language models (LLMs).

In this article we introduce a new tool, Papercheck, which uses text search, code, and large language models to extract information from scientific text (which could be a draft of a manuscript, submitted or published articles, or preregistration documents) and provide automated suggestions for improvement. Papercheck is inspired by quality control processes in software development. For example, R package developers run a set of automated checks before they submit their package to the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN). The automated checks aim to identify any remaining issues, and inform developers about how to fix them. The goal of papercheck is to screen scientific manuscripts, identify areas for improvement based on algorithms that emulate what experts would do while checking a research paper, and educate researchers on how to incorporate best practices. The tool is module based, with a dedicated module for any practice that the community wants to improve, and where automation offers a solution. This means the tool can be extended by the scientific community to fit their needs, and specialised modules can be created for different scientific fields based on what is considered a best practice in that research area. The tool can reduce the burden on peer reviewers by resolving common problems before submission, allowing peer reviewers to focus on those issues that can not be automatically detected.

Automated checks can quite accurately identify the presence or absence of information that should be reported (e.g., is the desired level of power reported in an a-priori power analysis), but a bigger challenge is to evaluate whether the provided information is valid (e.g., is there a good justification for the effect size entered in an a-priori power analysis). Papercheck focuses on the first task, and leaves the evaluation to the user. We will illustrate the potential of automated checks to improve best practices in 4 areas, namely 1) experimental design, 2) open science practices, 3) statistical inferences, and 4) reporting guidelines. Finally, we will demonstrate the usefulness of a tool that can efficiently process text in scientific articles to perform menial tasks (e.g., check if if hyperlinks are working), more easily code information from scientific articles for meta-scientific research, and incorporate existing automated checks (e.g., statcheck, checking if retracted articles are cited) in a single module-based workflow that can be expanded by the scientific community.


## Use Cases

The current version of Papercheck has two contexts of use. The first use-case is by scientists -- either authors or reviewers -- who have the goal to improve a scientific manuscript by checking for the presence or absence of specific practices. Papercheck can provide recommendations that improve the manuscript in situations where 1) a practice is not sufficiently salient to the scientist to be noticed without assistance, 2) the scientist is not yet able to identify the absence of a practice manually due to a lack of knowledge or training, or 3) scientists do not have time to identify the practice manually. Scientists using Papercheck are aware that all modules make recommendations that can be Type 1 and Type 2 errors. This means that it is possible that many possibly problematic practices are automatically identified, while none are actually problematic upon closer inspection. It is also possible that no problematic practices are found, but many are present.

As developers, our priority is to develop modules with error rates that are low enough to not impact the usability of Papercheck for individual authors, which - following the ISO 9241-11 definition - means "the extent to which a product can be used by specified users to achieve specified goals with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction in a specified context of use". Our working assumption is that preparing a scientific manuscript takes a considerable amount of time, and that scientists care about the quality of their work. Under this assumption, we believe that a tool with high error rates - say up to 50% - will be considered sufficiently useful to be adopted as long as it accurately identified some bad practices that researchers would not have identified themselves. For example, a spelling checker that marks 'Papercheck' and 'manuscirpt' as words with spelling errors, and does not mark 'extend' as a spelling error where the correct word would have been 'extent' remains useful as long as it takes relatively little time to evaluate the suggestions, even though the error rate is 2 out of 3.

The second use-case of Papercheck is as a tool to examine a large number of scientific articles. For example, a university or science funder might be interested in how many manuscripts by researchers that they employ or fund share data and code if this is in line with their policies. A meta-scientist might be interested in how many articles report effect sizes in a specific literature, and test whether there is an improvement in best practices. A scientific journal might want to evaluate how a change in editorial practices has impacted the diversity in populations that are examined in the studies they publish. Papercheck modules can easily be run on large numbers of papers, facilitating text searches and the automatic extraction and classification of information. In this use-case the usability of an automated tool requires low error rates if users want to use the output of the tool. Here, Type 2 errors are problematic, and difficult to identify, as it requires users to manually screen all papers for instances that were missed by the algorithms, and if manual screening was possible, there was no need for an automated tool. Type 1 errors might be easier to identify, but still require manually checking all instances flagged by a module. Therefore, low error rates are important for the usability of Papercheck as a meta-scientific tool. Validation procedures that quantify error rates are essential to safeguard the accuracy of results, and allow users to evaluate whether modules are accurate enough for their purposes, and communicate the error rates when presenting results. It is possible that a module has low-enough error rates for the individual use-case, while error rates are too high for meta-scientific use-cases.

# Examples

## Modules

### Automatically Checking Journal Article Reporting Standards

The journal article reporting standards (JARS) developed by the American Psychological Association (APA) offer guidance on the information that should be reported in scientific articles to enhance their scientific rigour (Appelbaum et al. 2018). Almost every published article would improve if researchers diligently followed JARS. However, the guidelines are not widely known, rarely implemented by authors, and almost never checked by editors or reviewers. Manually checking whether all reporting standards are implemented would be effortful. Automation can help by automatically checking if recommendations are followed.

The first reporting guideline that has been implemented in Papercheck is to report exact p-values. The APA Manual states:

> Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p \< .001.

Access to precisely reported p-values allows readers to include the test results in p value meta-analytic tests, such as p-curve, or z-curve (Simonsohn, Nelson, and Simmons 2014; Bartoš and Schimmack 2020), and makes it possible to the check the internal coherence of the reported results with tools such as Statcheck (Nuijten et al. 2015). Papercheck has a dedicated module, `exact_p`, to identify the presence of imprecise p-values. It will return all instances of imprecisely reported p-values in a paper.

We can also examine the difference between significant and non-significant effects, out of interest, and which imprecise p-values are reported. This illustrates how papercheck makes it possible to easily explore larger numbers of papers, and their properties. This allows us to uncover interesting explorative findings, such as the fact that there is a large peak at p \> 0.25, as it is apparently common for researchers to use this cut-off to indicate a non-significant result. It is unclear to us where this shared practice originates.

```{r}
res_imprecise <- module_run(xml, "exact_p")
res_imprecise$table$significance <- ifelse((res_imprecise$table$p_comp == "<"), "significant", "nonsignificant")

merged_data <- res_imprecise$table %>%
  group_by(id, significance) %>%
  summarise(
    imprecise_text = list(text),  # Store as a list (vector)
    total_imprecise = n(),        # Count number of entries
    .groups = "drop"              # Removes grouping in output
  )

# Rename only the specific columns in merged_data to avoid conflicts during the merge
significant_data <- merged_data %>%
  filter(significance == "significant") %>%
  rename(
    imprecise_text_significant = imprecise_text,
    total_imprecise_significant = total_imprecise
  )

nonsignificant_data <- merged_data %>%
  filter(significance == "nonsignificant") %>%
  rename(
    imprecise_text_nonsignificant = imprecise_text,
    total_imprecise_nonsignificant = total_imprecise
  )

# Merge each subset with psych_science
psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  left_join(significant_data[, c("id", "imprecise_text_significant", "total_imprecise_significant")], by = c("id" = "id"))

psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  left_join(nonsignificant_data[, c("id", "imprecise_text_nonsignificant", "total_imprecise_nonsignificant")], by = c("id" = "id"))

# Calculate percentage of papers with at least one 'total_marginal' per year
summary_df_nonsig <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_imprecise = sum(total_imprecise_nonsignificant > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_imprecise / total_papers) * 100
  )

# Calculate percentage of papers with at least one 'total_marginal' per year
summary_df_sig <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_imprecise = sum(total_imprecise_significant > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_imprecise / total_papers) * 100
  )

# Create grouped bar plot

imprecise_df <- psych_science %>%

  filter(!sapply(imprecise_text_nonsignificant, is.null)) %>%  # Remove NULLs
  unnest_longer(imprecise_text_nonsignificant) %>%

# Step 2: Extract numeric part from "p < .05", "p > .1", etc.

  scale_x_continuous(name = "Extracted p-value", limits = c(0, 1), breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.05)) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Imprecise p-values", y = "Frequency") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The peak at 0.25 is due to the tendency of authors to treat *p* values \> 0.25 as an indication of an absence of an effect. It is unclear where this criterion comes from. A possible origin might be the proposed alpha of 0.25 $\le$ $\alpha$ $\le$ 0.35 for stopping rules in forward stepwise selection procedures [@bendel1977comparison], later popularized as $\alpha$ $\le$ .025 in a widely used textbook on logistic regression [@hosmer2013applied], but we are unsure about this. The correct approach to conclude meaningful effects are absent is by performing an equivalence test against a smallest effect size of interest [@lakens_equivalence_2018].

### Reporting effect sizes

A second JARS guideline that can be automatically checked is whether people report effect sizes alongside their test result. Each test (e.g., a *t*-test, *F*-test, etc.) should include the corresponding effect size (e.g., a Cohen's *d*, or partial eta-squared). Based on a text search that uses regular expressions (regex), we can identify *t*-tests and *F*-tests that are not followed by an effect size, and warn researchers accordingly.

We have manually checked the *t*-tests and *F*-tests in 250 papers in Psychological Science, and our `effect_size` module detected 100% of *t*-tests with effect sizes, 99% of *t*-tests without effect sizes, 99% of *F*-tests with effect sizes, and 100% of *F*-tests without effect sizes. This is accurate enough to use the module for meta-scientific research, such as examining whether there is an increase in the best practice to report effect sizes for *t*-tests and *F*-tests over time. In the plot below we have run the module on 1838 published articles in the journal Psychological Science between 2014 and 2024. We can see that where a decade ago, around 25% of articles report *t*-tests or *F*-tests without an effect size this has dropped to between 10% and 15% a decade later. Perhaps a tool like Papercheck can reduce this percentage even further.

```{r}
res_effect_size <- module_run(xml, "effect_size")

psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  left_join(res_effect_size$summary)

# combined plot
# Summarise t-tests without effect sizes
summary_t <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_no_es = sum(ttests_without_es > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_no_es / total_papers) * 100
  ) %>%
  mutate(test_type = "t-test")

# Summarise F-tests without effect sizes
summary_f <- psych_science %>%
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    total_papers = n(),
    papers_with_no_es = sum(Ftests_without_es > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    percentage = (papers_with_no_es / total_papers) * 100
  ) %>%
  mutate(test_type = "F-test")

# Combine both summaries
combined_summary <- bind_rows(summary_t, summary_f)

# Create grouped bar plot
ggplot(combined_summary, aes(x = factor(year), y = percentage, fill = test_type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", position = "dodge", color = "black") +
  labs(title = "Papers with t-tests or F-tests Without Effect Sizes",
       x = "Year",
       y = "Percentage of Papers (%)",
       fill = "Test Type") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("t-test" = "skyblue", "F-test" = "orange")) +
  theme_minimal()

```

### Checking Data and Code in Repositories

There is widespread support among scientists for open science practices, such as data and code sharing [@ferguson2023survey]. There is increasing awareness of the importance of making data and code available alongside publication, and sometimes this is even a requirement by funders or journals. As data and code sharing is a relatively new practice, and many scientists lack training in open science, it is common to see badly documented data repositories. Best practices exist, such as the [TIER protocol](https://www.projecttier.org/tier-protocol/protocol-4-0/), but not all researchers might be aware of best practices. By automatically checking data repositories, Papercheck can increase awareness of best practices, and make specific suggestions for improvements.

At a minimum a data repository should contain a Read Me file with instructions for how to reproduce the results. If data is shared, it should be stored in a 'data' folder, or at least have the word 'data' in the filename. Code or scripts should similarly be shared in a folder with that name, or at least with the word in the filename. Finally, if data is shared, there should be a codebook or data dictionary that explains which variables are in the dataset in order to allow others to re-use the data. Ideally peer reviewers or editors would check the contents of a data repository. In practice, time constraints mean that data repository are often not checked by any human. Automation can perform some of the checks that peers might otherwise perform manually.

We will illustrate the process of checking a data repository by focusing on projects on the [Open Science Framework](www.osf.io). We start by searching for OSF URLs using the `osf_links` function. OSF links can be tricky to find in PDFs, since they can insert spaces in odd places, and view-only links that contain a ? are often interpreted as being split across sentences. This function is our best attempt at catching and fixing them all.

```{r search_osf}
links <- osf_links(xml)
```

If valid, the link is processed, and the OSF Application Programming Interface (API) is used to retrieve whether the link points to a file, project, or registration. This is achieved through the `osf_retrieve()` function. This function will retrieve all child components, files and folders if the argument `recursive = TRUE` is specified, and if the argument `find_project = TRUE` is specified, it will also look up the parent project of any links.

```{r osf_retrieve}
# osf_api_calls()
# osf_delay(delay = 2)
# info <- osf_retrieve(links, recursive = TRUE, find_project = TRUE)
# saveRDS(info, file = "all_osf_file_info_psych_science.rds")
```

We can then use this information to determine if, for each file, the information about the files contains text that makes it easy to determine what is being shared. A simple regular expression text search for 'README', 'codebook', 'script', and 'data' (in a number of possible ways that these words can be written) is used to automatically detect what is shared.

```{r summarize_osf_files}
osf_files_summary <- summarize_contents(all_osf_file_info_psych_science)

# Remove rows referring to badges
osf_files_summary <- subset(osf_files_summary, is.na(text) | !(text %in% c("osf.io/tvyxz/", "osf.io/tvyxz")))

# Create a dataframe with unique rows based on both osf_id and download_url
unique_files <- osf_files_summary[!duplicated(osf_files_summary["osf_id"]), ]

# Count occurrences of each osf_id
id_counts <- table(unique_files$osf_id)

# Get osf_ids that appear more than once
duplicate_ids <- names(id_counts[id_counts > 1])

# Should be 0
length(duplicate_ids)

registrations_only <- subset(unique_files, osf_type == "registrations")
files_only <- subset(unique_files, osf_type == "files")

# Count in the unique_files dataframe how many view_only links are published. Say we can screen for these. 
# Count how many links we find in the articles are on private. They need to be found as text (so text is no NA) and then public should be set to TRUE
# Count how many papers have at least one linked preregistration over time. I think Lisa should have a function to add these to the main dataframe? 




```

So far we have used Papercheck to check whether links exist, are publicly available, and whether certain types of files exist. But it is also possible to automatically download files, examine their contents, and provide feedback to users. This can be useful to examine datasets (e.g., do files contain IP addresses or other personal information), or code files. Papercheck also contains a function `osf_file_download` to download all files from a project on the OSF while maintaining the folder structure. This should make it easier for reviewers to manually check all content shared on the OSF.

### Checking Preregistrations

It is increasingly common for researchers to preregister their studies [@spitzer2023registered; @imai2025pre]. As preregistration is a new practice, it is not surprising that researchers do not perform preregistrations following the state-of-the-art. One challenge is that researchers deviate from their preregistration when reporting results from preregistered studies, but do not transparently report these deviations [@van2024potential]. Reviewers could check whether researchers adhere to the preregistration, but this requires some effort. Automation can provide a partial solution by making information from the preregistration more easily available.

Here we demonstrate how Papercheck can automatically retrieve the content of a preregistration. The preregistration can then be presented alongside the relevant information in the manuscript. This makes it easier for peer reviewers to compare the information.

We focus on AsPredicted preregistrations as their structured format makes it especially easy to retrieve information

### Checking Power Analyses

Researchers should provide a sample size justification when they design a study to provide an argument why the study has sufficient informational value with respect to its inferential goal [@lakens_justification_2022]. One approach to a sample size justification is a power analysis. Peers need to be able to evaluate the power analysis to examine with the arguments for the informational value of the study design are valid. This requires that all parameters of the power analysis are reported: The type of power analysis (e.g., a-priori, comprimise, sensitivity), the statistical test that the power analysis is performed for (e.g., an independent t-test, a within-between interaction effect in a 2x2 ANOVA), the effect size metric (e.g., d, r, odds ratio), the effect size (a numerical value, e.g., 0.3), the desired power (e.g., 95%), and the alpha level (commonly 0.05, but it is possible that this value needs to be adjusted for multiple comparisons). Many power analyses do not report all the required information. Moreover, some researchers perform post-hoc power analyses where they compute the power for the observed effect size, given the collected sample size. This flawed practice is performed in an attempt to answer the question whether a non-significant result is a Type 2 error, which post-hoc power can not answer.

The powercheck module aims to assist researchers in fully reporting power analysis, and dissuade them from performing a post-hoc power analysis. It first searches for the word "power\[ed\]", and based on a pre-trained local logistic regression model classifies sentences as a statistical power analysis, or not. Sentences classified as probable power analysis statements are then expanded by including the previous and two subsequent sentences, and sent to Groq, a service for artificial intelligence inference. Groq can run a range of different language models, such as Llama 3.3 70B, an open source language model. Based on a prompt the Groq API returns a JSON structured dataset with either the content of the parameters that should be reported in a power analysis, or missing information if the language model can not retrieve the values for certain parameters.

The information retrieved from the language model is then cleaned (e.g., by removing spaces) and standardized (e.g., Cohen's d, ds, and Hedges' g are all recoded as 'd', 0.8, 80%, and .80 are recoded as 0.80, etc.). An additional simple text search for words such as 'post-hoc power' or 'observed power' is performed. Based on this information users are informed about which parameters were not automatically identified, or why observed power analyses should not be informed. Given the complexity of natural language, we should expect Type 1 and type 2 errors. For an example , the sentence "Null of 33% power Note: The observed p -curve includes 29 statistically significant (p \< .05) results, of which 14 are p \< .025. There were 8 additional results entered but excluded from p-curve because they were p \> .05." was incorrectly classified as a sentence describing a power analysis (i.e., a Type 1 error) dus to the presence of a significance level threshold, and numbers of entities included and excluded in the analysis. The following sentence is an example of a Type 2 error: "We attempted to recruit 200 participants to have sufficient power to detect a small to moderate effect size, but in recruiting groups of friends on campus, we ended up with 199 fluent English speakers (105 female)". This statement provides too minimal information about the details of the power analysis to be classified as one.

Type 1 errors are annoying, but this annoyance is hopefully in the long run compensated by the benefits of a tool such as papercheck. Type 2 errors miss an opportunity to inform users of best practices. However, it is possible to still report the result of the power module by stating that no reported power analyses were identified, and informing users that if this is incorrect, they might want to reconsider whether the way they reported the power analysis is clear enough for human readers. A statement such as "We performed an a-priori power analysis for a one-sided dependent t-test with an alpha of 0.05, a desired power of 0.95, an effect size of interest of dz = 0.2, which lead to a required sample size of N = 272" should have a very high probability of being automatically detected and should allow all parameters to be automatically retrieved by the algorithm. Out of all 707 power analysis statements (although these include some double counted due to overlapping sentences) 72 were fully reported. Some missing information might not be considered too problematic, such as the alpha level which is almost exclusively 5% (although some researchers used 0.01 or corrected the alpha level for multiple comparisons) or the test (which can sometimes - although too often not - be retrieved from the result section. The simple warning for observed power based simply on a regex text search would catch the use of 'post-hoc' power in 45 instances across 37 papers. This bad practice is a rare occurrence, but flaw is relatively serious, and hence worth correcting through an automated tool.

```{r}
# Load required package
library(writexl)

text_found_power <- search_text(xml, "power(ed)?\\b", return = "sentence")

# Read in manually validated data (subset of total above)
coded_power <- read_xlsx("power_validate_search_power_2_5_2025_completed.xlsx")
coded_power$id <- sub("\\.xml$", "", coded_power$id)

# Remove results from a metascience paper by Bakker. It will confuse the logistic regression classifier.  
coded_power <- coded_power[coded_power$id != "0956797616647519", ]
# Expand the text
coded_power <- expand_text(coded_power, xml, expand_to = "sentence", plus = 1)


# Create a logistic regression classifier (Code by Lisa)
train <- dplyr::slice_sample(coded_power, prop = 0.5)
test <- anti_join(coded_power, train, by = "text")

# words <- distinctive_words(
#   text = train$text,
#   classification = train$power_computation,
#   n = 20,
#   numbers = "specific",
#   stop_words = c("the", "a", "of", "an", "and", "in", "we", "to", "with", "were", "et", "al")
# )

has_symbols <- c(has_equals = "=", 
                 has_percent = "%",
                 has_80 = ".80",
#                 has_80percent = "80%",
                 has_90percent = "90%",
                 has_apriori = "a priori",
                 has_eta = "η p 2",
                 has_cohend = "Cohen's d",
                 has_gpower = "G*Power")

power_words <- c("power", "size", "sampl", "particip", "detect", "analys", "05", "α")

# Only text

features <- text_features(
  text = train$text, 
  words = power_words,
  word_count = FALSE, 
  has_number = TRUE,
  has_symbol = has_symbols,
  values = "presence" # presence or count
)

# show the first row
features[1, ] |> str()

# Train logistic regression model

model <- glm(train$power_computation ~ .,
             data = features,
             family = "binomial")

summary(model)

train$model_response <- predict(model, features)

train$power_computation_predict <-
  train$model_response > 0.5

dplyr::count(train, 
             power_computation, 
             power_computation_predict)

test_features <- text_features(
  text = test$text, 
  words = power_words,
  word_count = FALSE, 
  has_number = TRUE,
  has_symbol = has_symbols, 
  values = "presence" # presence or count
)
test$model_response <- predict(model, test_features)

test$power_computation_predict <-
  test$model_response > 0.5

dplyr::count(test, 
             power_computation, 
             power_computation_predict)

# Add column to easily check matches and mismatches
test$match_result <- ifelse(
  as.logical(test$power_computation) == test$power_computation_predict,
  "correct",
  "false"
)

train$match_result <- ifelse(
  as.logical(train$power_computation) == train$power_computation_predict,
  "correct",
  "false"
)


# Expanded

features <- text_features(
  text = train$expanded, 
  words = power_words,
  word_count = FALSE, 
  has_number = TRUE,
  has_symbol = has_symbols,
  values = "presence" # presence or count
)

# show the first row
features[1, ] |> str()

# Train logistic regression model

model <- glm(train$power_computation ~ .,
             data = features,
             family = "binomial")

summary(model)

train$model_response_expanded <- predict(model, features)

train$power_computation_predict_expanded <-
  train$model_response_expanded > 0.5

dplyr::count(train, 
             power_computation, 
             power_computation_predict_expanded)

test_features <- text_features(
  text = test$expanded, 
  words = power_words,
  word_count = FALSE, 
  has_number = TRUE,
  has_symbol = has_symbols, 
  values = "presence" # presence or count
)
test$model_response_expanded <- predict(model, test_features)

test$power_computation_predict_expanded <-
  test$model_response_expanded > 0.5

dplyr::count(test,

# Add column to easily check matches and mismatches

# Now run this on the psych_science dataset

```

Now we ask an LLM to process the power analysis statements.

```{r}
# Define the query
query <- paste0(
  "You will be given a piece of academic text. Your task is to:\n\n",
  "1. **Classify** the type of power analysis mentioned:\n",
  "   - \"a priori\": if power analysis is done before data collection to determine sample size.\n",
  "   - \"post hoc\": if power is computed after observing the results (e.g., effect size, p-values).\n",
  "   - \"unclear\": if it's not clear whether the power analysis is pre- or post-data.\n",
  "   - \"no power analysis\": if there's no mention of power analysis.\n\n",
  "2. **Extract the following fields**, but only if the classification is \"a priori\" or \"post-hoc\":\n\n",
  "   - \"statistical_test\": What statistical test is used (e.g., ANOVA, t-test).\n",
  "   - \"alpha_level\": The alpha level (e.g., 0.05).\n",
  "   - \"effect_size\": The numeric effect size used.\n",
  "   - \"type_effect_size\": The type of effect size (e.g., standardized mean differences (indicated by the letter d for between designs, and d z for within designs), or by for example the letters f, η² or η p 2, etc.).\n",
  "   - \"desired_power\": The target statistical power (e.g., 0.80, 0.90, or 80%, 95%).\n",
  "   - \"total_sample_size\": The total sample size specified or required.\n\n",
  "Use \"unknown\" if any of the values are not specified. Always return a valid JSON object in the following format, making such all \"and { and } are present:\n\n",
  "{\n",
  "  \"classification\": \"a priori\" | \"post hoc\" | \"unclear\" | \"no power analysis\",\n",
  "  \"statistical_test\": \"x\",\n",
  "  \"alpha_level\": \"x\",\n",
  "  \"effect_size\": \"x\",\n",
  "  \"type_effect_size\": \"x\",\n",
  "  \"desired_power\": \"x\",\n",
  "  \"total_sample_size\": \"x\"\n",
  "}\n"
)


# Define batch size
llm_max_calls(n = 800)
batch_size <- 100
text_found_power$llm_result <- NA_character_  # Ensures it's a character column

# Get total number of rows
total_rows <- nrow(text_found_power)
starting_row <- 1

# Filter rows where power_computation_predict is TRUE
rows_to_process <- which(text_found_power$power_computation_predict)

# Total rows to process
total_rows <- length(rows_to_process)

# Loop in batches
for (j in seq(801, total_rows, by = batch_size)) {
  
  # Define batch range
  batch_end <- min(j + batch_size - 1, total_rows)
  batch_indices <- rows_to_process[j:batch_end]
  
  # Select batch of text
  text_batch <- text_found_power$expanded[batch_indices]
  
  # Try sending requests to LLM
  tryCatch({
    res <- llm(text_batch, query)  # Call the LLM
    
    # Store the results
    text_found_power$llm_result[batch_indices] <- res$answer  
    
    # Print progress
    cat("Completed batch indices:", j, "to", batch_end, "\n")
    
    # Ask whether to continue
    continue <- readline(prompt = "Do you want to continue? (Y/N): ")
    
    if (tolower(continue) == "n") {
      cat("You can continue later starting from batch index:", j + batch_size, "\n")
      break
    }
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat("Error at batch indices:", j, "to", batch_end, "\n")
    cat("Error message:", e$message, "\n")
    stop("Stopping script due to error.")
  })
}

filename <- paste0("data/power_lmm_expanded_", format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d_%H-%M-%S"), ".RData")

  paste0(text_found_power$llm_result, "}"),
  text_found_power$llm_result
)

text_found_power$llm_result[1110] <- "{\n  \"classification\": \"a priori\",\n  \"statistical_test\": \"analysis of variance\",\n  \"effect_size\": \"0.4\",\n  \"type_effect_size\": \"standard deviations\",\n  \"desired_power\": \"0.86\",\n  \"total_sample_size\": \"120\"\n}"

text_found_power$llm_result[1979] <- "{\n  \"classification\": \"a priori\",\n  \"statistical_test\": \"unknown\",\n  \"effect_size\": \"0.30\",\n  \"type_effect_size\": \"d\",\n  \"desired_power\": \"0.80\",\n  \"total_sample_size\": \"278\"\n}"

text_found_power$llm_result[2423] <- "{\n  \"classification\": \"post hoc\",\n  \"statistical_test\": \"F-test\",\n  \"alpha_level\": \"< .001\",\n  \"effect_size\": \".446, .395, .175\",\n  \"type_effect_size\": \"η p 2\",\n  \"desired_power\": \"unknown\",\n  \"total_sample_size\": \"198\"\n}"

text_found_power$llm_result[3662] <- "{\n  \"classification\": \"a priori\",\n  \"statistical_test\": \"unknown\",\n  \"alpha_level\": \"unknown\",\n  \"effect_size\": \"unknown\",\n  \"type_effect_size\": \"unknown\",\n  \"desired_power\": \"0.991, 0.801\",\n  \"total_sample_size\": \"350\"\n}"

# First create empty columns with the appropriate names
new_cols <- c("classification", "statistical_test", "alpha_level", "effect_size",
              "type_effect_size", "desired_power", "total_sample_size")

text_found_power[new_cols] <- NA

# Process each row
for (i in seq_len(nrow(text_found_power))) {
  print(i)
  json_text <- text_found_power$llm_result[i]
  
  if (!is.na(json_text) && nchar(json_text) > 0) {
    result <- fromJSON(json_text)
    
    # Assign each element to the corresponding new column
    for (col in new_cols) {
      if (!is.null(result[[col]])) {
        text_found_power[[col]][i] <- result[[col]]
      }
    }
  }
}
```

Now we can take a look at how often which info is missing, if power analyses increase over time, etc. We first merge everything into psych_science

```{r}
# Merge
# 1. Identify IDs with predicted power analysis
ids_with_power <- text_found_power %>%
  filter(power_computation_predict == TRUE) %>%
  distinct(id) %>%
  pull(id)

# 2. Aggregate power_text and expanded text per ID
power_rows <- text_found_power %>%
  filter(power_computation_predict == TRUE) %>%
  group_by(id) %>%
  summarise(
    power_text = list(text),
    power_text_expanded = list(expanded),
    classification = list(na.omit(classification)),
    statistical_test = list(na.omit(statistical_test)),
    alpha_level = list(na.omit(alpha_level)),
    effect_size = list(na.omit(effect_size)),
    type_effect_size = list(na.omit(type_effect_size)),
    desired_power = list(na.omit(desired_power)),
    total_sample_size = list(na.omit(total_sample_size)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(
    classification:total_sample_size,
    ~ map(.x, ~ if(length(.x) == 0) NA else .x)
  ))

# 3. Join and assign has_power_analysis based on ID presence
psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  left_join(power_rows, by = "id") %>%
  mutate(has_power_analysis = id %in% ids_with_power)

# save(psych_science, file = "psych_science_with_power_expanded.RData")
load(file = "psych_science_with_power_expanded.RData")

# Clean up data

psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  mutate(
    type_effect_size = map(type_effect_size, function(x) {
      if (is.null(x) || length(x) == 0) return(NULL)
      
      # Replace your patterns first
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\bd\\s?z\\b", "dz")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\bcorrelation\\s?coefficient\\b", "r")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\bhedges['’]?s\\s?g\\b", "d")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\bcohen['’]?s\\s?d\\b", "d")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "η\\s?p\\s?2", "ηp2")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "f\\s?2", "f2")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "f\\s?²", "f2")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\bcohen['’]?s\\s?f²\\b", "f2")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\bcohen['’]?s\\s?f\\s?2\\b", "f2")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\bcohen['’]?s f\\b", "f")
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "(?i)\\br\\s?2\\b|\\br²\\b|\\br\\^2\\b|\\bR\\s?2\\b|\\bR²\\b|\\bR\\^2\\b", "r2")
      
      # Trim leading and trailing whitespace (spaces, tabs, newlines, etc.)
      x <- stri_trim_both(x)
      
      # Replace multiple internal whitespace (space, tab, newline) with a single space
      x <- str_replace_all(x, "\\s+", " ")
      
      # Remove any empty strings if they exist after trimming
      x <- x[x != ""]
      
      if (length(x) == 0) return(NULL)
      
      return(x)
    })
  )


# Clean desired_power

format_power_value <- function(x) {
  # Convert to numeric safely
  num <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(x))
  if (is.na(num)) return(NA_character_)
  # Format with 2 decimals and leading zero (sprintf always adds leading zero)
  sprintf("%.2f", num)
}

psych_science <- psych_science %>%
  mutate(
    desired_power = map(desired_power, ~ {
      if (is.null(.x) || length(.x) == 0) return(NULL)
      # Clean each value in the vector
      cleaned <- map_chr(.x, format_power_value)
      cleaned
    })
  )
```

What would our feedback from the papercheck app look like?

```{r}

check_power_analysis <- function(single_paper, verbose = FALSE) {
  cols_to_check <- c("classification", "power_text_expanded", "statistical_test", "alpha_level", "effect_size", "type_effect_size", "desired_power", "total_sample_size")
  
  analysis_fields <- c(
    "statistical_test", "alpha_level", "effect_size",
    "type_effect_size", "desired_power", "total_sample_size"
  )

  # Check that all columns are lists and have equal lengths
  list_lengths <- sapply(single_paper[cols_to_check], function(x) {
    if (is.null(x[[1]])) return(0)
    if (!is.list(x)) return(NA)
    length(x[[1]])
  })

  if (length(unique(list_lengths)) != 1 || any(is.na(unique(list_lengths)))) {
    msg <- paste0("⚠️ Row with ID ", single_paper$id, 
                  ": Not all power analysis columns contain the same number of items.")
    if (verbose) cat(msg, "\n\n")
    return(NULL)
  }

  # Expand and deduplicate
  expanded_df <- single_paper %>%
    mutate(row_id = 1) %>%
    unnest_longer(all_of(cols_to_check)) %>%
    distinct(across(all_of(analysis_fields)), .keep_all = TRUE) %>%
    group_by(row_id) %>%
    mutate(power_analysis_number = paste0("power analysis ", row_number())) %>%
    ungroup()

  # Message prefix for multiple analyses
  if (nrow(expanded_df) > 1 && verbose) {
    cat(paste0("Papercheck identified ", nrow(expanded_df), " power analysis statements.\n\n"))
  }

  # Loop through each analysis row and collect messages
  power_summaries <- vector("character", length = nrow(expanded_df))

  for (i in seq_len(nrow(expanded_df))) {
    row <- expanded_df[i, ]

    msg <- case_when(
      is.null(row$power_text_expanded[[1]]) || all(is.na(row$power_text_expanded[[1]])) ~
        "We found no power analysis in this paper. If you intended to report a power analysis, it might need to be reported more systematically and completely to be automatically identified.",
      TRUE ~ paste(
        "Papercheck has identified the following text as a power analysis:",
        row$power_text_expanded[[1]],
        sep = "\n\n"
      )
    )

    # Identify missing fields
    missing_info <- cols_to_check[-1][
      sapply(row[cols_to_check[-1]], function(x) {
        val <- x[[1]]
        is.null(val) || is.na(val) || tolower(str_trim(val)) == "unknown"
      })
    ]

    # Append missing/completeness message
    if (length(missing_info) > 0) {
      msg <- paste(
        msg,
        crayon::red$bold("The following information was missing in the description of the power analysis, or not automatically identified:"),
        paste(missing_info, collapse = ", "),
        sep = "\n\n"
      )
    } else {
      msg <- paste(
        msg,
        crayon::green$bold("This power analysis is reported completely, including all information required to increase the probability that it can be independently replicated. If not done already, consider adding a link to computationally reproducible code for this power analysis, or a screenshot or report provided by the power analysis software you are using."),
        sep = "\n\n"
      )
    }

    # Add analysis header if needed
    if (nrow(expanded_df) > 1) {
      msg <- paste0("== ", row$power_analysis_number, " ==\n", msg)
    }

    # Save message
    power_summaries[i] <- msg

    # Conditionally print
    if (verbose) cat(msg, "\n\n---\n\n")
  }

  # Add message to dataframe
  expanded_df$power_summary <- power_summaries

  # Add reported columns
  for (field in analysis_fields) {
    expanded_df[[paste0(field, "_reported")]] <- !(
      is.na(expanded_df[[field]]) |
        tolower(trimws(expanded_df[[field]])) == "unknown"
    )
  }

  return(expanded_df)
}

# Now apply it to psych_science for rows with has_power_analysis

result_df <- psych_science %>%
  filter(has_power_analysis == TRUE) %>%
  split(1:nrow(.)) %>%
  map_dfr(check_power_analysis)  # map_dfr binds all returned dataframes together
```

```{r}
testset <- rbind(apriori_power[1:10, ], post_hoc_power)

observed_power_regex <- "(\\bobserved power\\b|\\bpost[ -]hoc power\\b|\\bretrospective power\\b|\\b(?:achieved(?:\\s+\\w+){0,2}\\s+power)\\b)"

# Add the new column based on regex match
testset <- testset %>%
  mutate(posthoc_regex_match = ifelse(str_detect(text, observed_power_regex), 1, 0))

# FIGURE OUT PRIVACY OF GROQ

# Define the query
query <- "Does this sentence describe what is known as 'observed power', or 'post-hoc power'? This would be true if the power directly follows statistical test results, or if power is computed for the results observed in the study. Return 'post hoc' if so. If the power analysis is done 'a priori', before data is collected, to determine the sample size of the study, answer 'a priori'. If it is unclear, return 'unclear', and if the statement is not about statistical power, return 'no power analysis'"

res <- llm(testset$text, query)

# Detect if "a priori" is in the answer
testset$result_apriori <- ifelse(grepl("\\ba priori\\b", res$answer), 1, 0)

# Detect if "post hoc" is in the answer
testset$result_posthoc <- ifelse(grepl("\\bpost[- ]hoc\\b", res$answer), 1, 0)

# Now we take the testset, only those classified as apriori, and get details by expanding the text, then asking llm.

apriori <- testset %>%
  filter(result_apriori == 1)

apriori <- expand_text(apriori, psych_oa_xml, plus = 2, minus = 2)

query <- paste0(
  "In the following text, a researcher describes an a priori power analysis. ",
  "A fully reported power analysis should specify the test researchers will perform, ",
  "the alpha level of the test, the effect size, the type of effect size (e.g., cohens's d, f, eta, omega), and the desired power. ",
  "This leads to the sample size they will collect. ",
  "Extract this information, be brief (answer only in numbers where possible), and format the output as a JSON object. {",
  "  \"statistical_test\": \"x\",",
  "  \"alpha_level\": \"x\",",
  "  \"effect_size\": \"x\",",
  "  \"type_effect_size\": \"x\",",
  "  \"desired_power\": \"x\",",
  "  \"total_sample_size\": \"x\"",
  "} ",
  "The text is:"
)

res_ex <- llm(apriori$expanded, query)

# Regular expression pattern to match key-value pairs including "total sample size"
pattern <- "\"(.*?)\":\\s*\"?([^,\n]+)\"?"

# Function to extract key-value pairs from the text
extract_info <- function(text) {
  # Extract key-value pairs using the regex pattern
  matches <- regmatches(text, gregexpr(pattern, text, perl = TRUE))
  
  # Flatten the list of matches
  key_value_pairs <- unlist(matches)
  
  # Check if key_value_pairs is empty
  if(length(key_value_pairs) == 0) {
    return(NULL)
  }
  
  # Extract keys and values separately
  keys <- gsub("\"(.*?)\":.*", "\\1", key_value_pairs)  # Extract key
  values <- gsub(".*?:\\s*\"?(.*)\"?", "\\1", key_value_pairs)  # Extract value
  
  # Return as a named list (key-value pairs)
  return(setNames(values, keys))
}

# Apply the extraction function to each text string
extracted_data <- lapply(res_ex$answer, function(x) {
  tryCatch({
    extract_info(x)
  }, error = function(e) {
    NULL  # Return NULL if an error occurs
  })
})

# Convert the list to a data frame
extracted_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(extracted_data, function(x) as.data.frame(t(x))))

# Function to clean each cell
clean_cell <- function(x) {
  x <- trimws(x)                        # Remove leading & trailing spaces
  x <- gsub("\"", "", x)                # Remove all double quotes
  x <- ifelse(tolower(x) %in% c("not specified", "", "na"), NA, x) # Convert "not specified" and empty values to NA
  return(x)
}

# Apply the cleaning function to all cells in the dataframe
extracted_df <- extracted_df %>% mutate_all(clean_cell)

final_apriori <- cbind(apriori, res_ex[2:4], extracted_df)

# Function to compute power analysis for t-test
compute_power <- function(statistical_test, effect_size, alpha_level, desired_power) {
  if (tolower(statistical_test) %in% c("t test", "t-test")) {
    result <- pwr::pwr.t.test(d = as.numeric(effect_size), sig.level = as.numeric(alpha_level), power = as.numeric(desired_power), type ="two.sample", alternative = "two.sided")
    sample_size <- 2*ceiling(result$n)
    return(sample_size)  # Store the sample size required
  } else {
    return(NA)  # If not a t-test, return NA
  }
}

# Apply function row-wise
final_apriori <- final_apriori %>%
  mutate(reproduced_power = pmap_dbl(
    list(statistical_test, effect_size, alpha_level, desired_power),
    compute_power
  ))

# View the result
print(final_apriori)



```

### Text search

### Hyperlinks

Many scientific articles link to additional information that is not included in the article, such as open data, materials, and code, a preregistration, or supplementary information. Although it is useful to have access to this information, it can also be cumbersome to retrieve it. Journals lack a systematic way of providing access to information outside of the article, and the additional information that is provided is often not structured well. Although this is expected as science transitions to more transparency, the fact that supplementary information is often not easily findable or accessible limits its use. Automation can assists researchers by making information more readily available.

One starting point to retrieve information is a hyperlink. We can retrieve hyperlinks from pdf articles in two ways. First, GROBID automatically extracts hyperlinks (i.e., text that can be clicked to open an external website). Second, regular expressions can identify hyperlinks that can not be clicked based on common text patterns in hyperlinks (e.g., the presence of http or www, followed by a string of characters). To capture all hyperlinks it is often necessary to iteratively search the text. Text parsing often struggles with hyperlinks, and it is common to see line breaks in hyperlinks that result in hyperlinks being split across two sentences or having spaces in the hyperlink that need to be removed. Identifying and fixing hyperlinks requires knowledge about the structure of hyperlinks (e.g., links to the Open Science Framework or AsPredicted have either 5 or 6 characters after the domain).

We will provide two illustrations of the usefulness of combining domain expertise with automatically detecting hyperlinks. The first example pertains to the presence of links to anonymized files that are used during the peer review process in published articles. Many journals anonymize authors, which requires linking to anonymized supplementary files. This can be achieved on AsPredicted through a special 'blind' link (e.g., https://aspredicted.org/blind.php?x=5tq3pg) or a 'view_only' link to the OSF. Sometimes, these links make it into the published article, even though they should be replaced by the public link after acceptance.

```{r}

```

```{r}

RGX_ASPREDICTED <- "aspredicted"
text_found <- search_text(xml, RGX_ASPREDICTED, return = "paragraph")
# blind links often end up having a space in the extracted hyperlink. 
# e.g., https://aspredicted.org/blind.php? x=6uq6sx which should have been extracted as https://aspredicted.org/blind.php?x=6uq6sx
# So we fix it by removing the space. 
text_found$text <- gsub("blind\\.php\\?\\s*", "blind.php?", text_found$text)
RGX_ASPREDICTED_LINK <- "aspredicted\\.org/\\s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{5}"
text_found_as_predicted <- search_text(text_found, RGX_ASPREDICTED_LINK, return = "match")
RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND <- "http://aspredicted\\.org/blind\\.php\\?x=s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{6}"
text_found_as_predicted_blind <- search_text(text_found, RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND, return = "match")

RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND <- "http://aspredicted\\.org/blind\\.php\\?x=s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{6}"
text_found_as_predicted_blind <- search_text(text_found, RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND, return = "match")

# Remove duplicates
text_found_as_predicted_blind <- text_found_as_predicted_blind %>% distinct(text, .keep_all = TRUE)
```

### OSF Links

```{r}
# Define the regular expression pattern for detecting OSF URLs 
# We first find any osf link to fix some not completely caught
RGX_OSF <- "osf\\.io"
text_found <- search_text(xml, RGX_OSF, return = "sentence")
text_found$text <- gsub("(osf.io/)>\\s*", "\\1", text_found$text)

# We take advantage of the fact that OSF URL's have a specific format.
RGX_OSF <- "osf\\.io/\\s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{5}"
text_found <- search_text(text_found, RGX_OSF, return = "match")

RGX_VIEWONLY <- "view_only"
text_found <- search_text(xml, RGX_VIEWONLY, return = "paragraph")
text_found$text <- gsub("/\\? view_only", "/?view_only", text_found$text)

RGX_VIEWONLY <- "osf\\.io/\\s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{5}/(?:files/)?\\?view_only"
text_found <- search_text(text_found, RGX_VIEWONLY, return = "match")

```

We clean up the links we have found, and extract the OSF ID:

```{r}
text_found <- distinct(text_found, text, .keep_all = TRUE)
# Add https if missing from URL
text_found$http_osf <- tolower(ifelse(grepl("^https?://", text_found$text), text_found$text, paste0("https://", text_found$text)))
# Add extract only the 6 character OSF id from the URL
text_found$osf_id <- tolower(substr(text_found$text, 8, 12))
```

We can now check if the OSF view_only link goes to a page that is still closed.

```{r}
# link <- "bc8yg"
# Initialize OSF project name and ID
text_found$osf_project_name <- NA
text_found$osf_project_id <- NA
text_found$osf_type <- NA

# Loop through each osf_id
for (i in 1:nrow(text_found)) {
  link <- text_found$osf_id[i]  # Get the osf_id
  osf_project_id <- NULL
  # Strip it to only have the osf code
  osf_id <- as_id(link)  # Ensure as_id function is defined

  # Get the osf_project_id with error handling
  # Check if it is a node
  osf_project_id <- tryCatch(
    osf_retrieve_node(osf_id),
    error = function(e) {
      return(NULL)  # Return NULL if retrieval fails
      print("fail 1")
    })
  # Store the results in the data frame
  if (!is.null(osf_project_id)) {
    text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- osf_project_id[1]
    text_found$osf_type[i] <- "project"
    # Store the results in the data frame
    if (!is.null(osf_project_id)) {
      root_project <- osf_project_id[[3]][[1]][["relationships"]][["root"]][["data"]][["id"]]
      osf_project_id <- tryCatch(
        osf_retrieve_node(root_project)[2], # return root id if public
        error = function(e) {
          return(osf_project_id[2])  # Return node id if retrieval fails
          print("root id closed, saving node id")
        })
      text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- osf_project_id
      text_found$osf_type[i] <- "project"
    }
  }

  # Check if it is a file
  if (is.null(osf_project_id)) {
    osf_project_id <- tryCatch(
      osf_retrieve_file(osf_id),
      error = function(e) {
        return(NULL)  # Return NULL if retrieval fails
      })
    # Store the results in the data frame
    if (!is.null(osf_project_id)) {
      text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- osf_project_id[1]
      text_found$osf_type[i] <- "file"
      parent_project <- osf_project_id[[3]][[1]][["relationships"]][["node"]][["data"]][["id"]]
      osf_project_id <- tryCatch(
        osf_retrieve_node(parent_project), # return root id if public
        error = function(e) {
          return(osf_project_id)  # Return node id if retrieval fails
          print("root id closed, saving node id")
        })

      text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- osf_project_id[2]
      text_found$osf_type[i] <- "file"
      }
  }

  # Check if it is a registration
  if (is.null(osf_project_id)) {

    osf_project_id <- tryCatch(
      registration <- GET(paste("https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/?filter[id]=",link, sep = "")),
      error = function(e) {
        return(NULL)  # Return NULL if retrieval fails
      })
    registration <- fromJSON(rawToChar(registration$content))
    # Store the results in the data frame
    if (length(registration$data) != 0) {
      print("succes 3")
      description <- registration$data$attributes$title
      parent_project <- registration$data$relationships$registered_from$data$id
        # Get parent project
      parent_node  <- tryCatch(
        GET(paste(registration$data$relationships$registered_from$links$related$href)),
        error = function(e) {
          return(NULL)  # Return null if retrieval fails (but it always gets some data)
        })
      if (!is.null(parent_node)) {
        project <- fromJSON(rawToChar(parent_node$content))
        project_id <- ifelse(is.null(project$data$id), "NA", project$data$id)
        project_title <- ifelse(is.null(project$data$attributes$title), "NA", project$data$attributes$title)
        text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- project_title
        text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- project_id
        text_found$osf_type[i] <- "registration"
      }
    }
    # If the call to get data returns an empty list, it is closed
    if (length(registration$data) == 0) {
      text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- NA
        text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- NA
        text_found$osf_type[i] <- "CLOSED"
      
    }
  }
}
sum(text_found$osf_type == "CLOSED")
```

```{r}
        text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- project_title
        text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- project_id
        text_found$osf_type[i] <- "registration"
      }
    }
    # If the call to get data returns an empty list, it is closed
    if (length(registration$data) == 0) {
      text_found$osf_project_name[i] <- NA
        text_found$osf_project_id[i] <- NA
        text_found$osf_type[i] <- "CLOSED"
      
    }
  }
}
```

```{r}
# Load the dataframe text_found that contains all osf retrieved info.
load(file = "psychscience_osf_full.RData")

# Only select registrations
registration_df <- text_found %>%
  filter(osf_type == "registration")

  distinct(osf_id, .keep_all = TRUE)  #

categorize_preregistration <- function(prereg_id) {
  
  print("Waiting a second for rate limitations")
  Sys.sleep(5)

  # Step 1: Fetch registration data from the API
  registration <- tryCatch({
    GET(paste0("https://api.osf.io/v2/registrations/?filter[id]=", prereg_id))
  }, error = function(e) {
    print(paste("API request failed for", prereg_id, "-", e$message))
    return(NULL)  # Return NULL to indicate failure
  })
  
  # If API call failed, return an error result
  if (is.null(registration) || registration$status_code != 200) {
    print(paste("Failed to fetch data for", prereg_id, "- HTTP status:", registration$status_code))
    return(list(prereg_id = prereg_id, content = NA, result = "ERROR"))
  }
  
  # Step 3: Parse the JSON content
  registration_content <- tryCatch({
    fromJSON(rawToChar(registration$content))
  }, error = function(e) {
    print(paste("Failed to parse JSON for", prereg_id, "-", e$message))
    return(NULL)
  })

  # If JSON parsing failed, return an error
  if (is.null(registration_content) || !is.list(registration_content) || is.null(registration_content$data)) {
    print(paste("Invalid response structure for", prereg_id))
    return(list(prereg_id = prereg_id, content = NA, result = "ERROR"))
  }
  
  # Step 5: Extract metadata safely
  registered_meta <- registration_content$data$attributes$registered_meta
  if (is.null(registered_meta)) {
    print(paste("No registered_meta found for", prereg_id))
    return(list(prereg_id = prereg_id, content = NA, result = "ERROR"))
  }
  
  # Initialize a list to store rows for the dataframe
  df_rows <- list()

  # Loop through metadata and prepare rows
  for (q in names(registered_meta)) {
    value_entry <- registered_meta[[q]]$value  # Store value reference
    
    # Check if value_entry is a list and has the necessary nested structure
    if (is.list(value_entry) && 
        "question" %in% names(value_entry) && 
        "uploader" %in% names(value_entry) && 
        !is.null(value_entry$question$value) && 
        !is.na(value_entry$question$value)) {
      
      # Extract nested values safely
      question_value <- as.character(value_entry$question$value)
      uploader_value <- as.character(value_entry$uploader$value)
      
      df_rows[[q]] <- data.frame(
        question = q,
        main_value = question_value,
        uploader_value = uploader_value,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
      
    } else {
      # Fallback: Extract only the main value if the nested structure is missing
      main_value <- as.character(value_entry)
      
      df_rows[[q]] <- data.frame(
        question = q,
        main_value = main_value,
        uploader_value = NA,  # No uploader value for default cases
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      )
    }
  }

  # Combine rows into a single dataframe
  prereg_info_osf <- do.call(rbind, df_rows)

  # Collapse the content of main values
  collapsed_content <- paste(prereg_info_osf$main_value, collapse = " ")

  # Truncate to prevent errors in API call
  max_length <- 2000  # Adjust based on API limits
  collapsed_content <- substr(collapsed_content, 1, max_length)

  # Create the prompt for categorization
  prompt <- "Answer TRUE if the following text refers to a preregistration of a scientific study where researchers describe their hypotheses and planned analyses, or if they text only contains 'NO'. Answer FALSE if this text refers to creating a frozen version of a project related to a publication, indicated by, for example, a reference to the name of a scientific journal. The text is: "

  # Step 6: Send the prompt to the GPT-based API
  response_groq <- tryCatch({
    llm(text = collapsed_content, query = prompt)
  }, error = function(e) {
    print(paste("Failed to get response from GPT API for", prereg_id, "-", e$message))
    return("ERROR")
  })
  
  # Step 7: Extract TRUE or FALSE from the response
  result <- regmatches(response_groq, regexpr("\\b(TRUE|FALSE)\\b", response_groq))
  if (length(result) == 0) result <- "ERROR"  # Handle cases where no valid response is returned
  
  # Return the result as a list
  return(list(
    prereg_id = prereg_id,
    prereg_info_osf = prereg_info_osf,
    content = collapsed_content,
    result = result
  ))
}
```

```{r}
# We can not send too long text to Groq, so we trim the end. 
trim_text <- function(text, max_chars = 5950) {
  char_count <- nchar(text)/4
  if (char_count > max_chars) {
    message("Text is too long. Trimming to ", max_chars, " characters.")
    text <- substr(text, 1, max_chars)
  }
  return(text)
}
```

```{r}

# Function to process a single URL and extract data
process_url <- function(url) {
  # Get the HTML content
  page <- GET(url) %>% read_html()
  
  # Extract the text content
  text <- page %>% html_text2()

  # Regular expression pattern to split by one or more newlines or multiple spaces
  split_text <- unlist(strsplit(text, "\n"))
  
  # Remove empty lines and lines with only whitespace (including \r, \n, spaces)
  split_text <- split_text[nchar(gsub("\\s", "", split_text)) > 0]

  # Initialize a list to hold the answers
  answers <- list(
    title = split_text[2]
  )
  
  # Function to extract text for a question
  extract_question <- function(start_text, end_text, split_text) {
  # Wrap the function in tryCatch to handle errors
  result <- tryCatch({
    start_index <- grep(start_text, split_text)
    end_index <- grep(end_text, split_text)
    
    # Ensure both start and end indices are found
    if(length(start_index) == 0 || length(end_index) == 0) {
      stop("Start or end text not found")
    }
    
    # Extract the text between the start and end indices
    found_text <- split_text[(start_index + 1):(end_index - 1)]
    
    # Combine the text into a single string and return
    paste(found_text, collapse = " ")
    
  }, error = function(e) {
    # Return "ERROR" if any error occurs
    return("ERROR")
  })
  
  return(result)
}

  
  answers$created <- extract_question("Pre-registered on", "Have any data been collected", split_text)
  answers$authors <- extract_question("Author", "Pre-registered on", split_text)

  # Extract answers for Q1-Q8
  answers$Q1 <- extract_question("Have any data been collected", "What's the main question being asked or hypothesis being tested", split_text)
  answers$Q2 <- extract_question("What's the main question being asked or hypothesis being tested in this study?", "Describe the key dependent variable", split_text)
  answers$Q3 <- extract_question("Describe the key dependent variable", "How many and which conditions will", split_text)
  answers$Q4 <- extract_question("How many and which conditions will", "Specify exactly which analyses you will conduct", split_text)
  answers$Q5 <- extract_question("Specify exactly which analyses you will conduct", "Describe exactly how outliers will be defined|Any secondary analyses", split_text)
  answers$Q6 <- extract_question("Describe exactly how outliers will be defined|Any secondary analyses", "How many observations will be collected", split_text)
  answers$Q7 <- extract_question("number will be determined", "Anything else you would like to pre-register", split_text)
  answers$Q8 <- extract_question("secondary analyses, variables collected", "Version of AsPredicted Questions", split_text)
  
  # Extract version
  version_index <- grep("Version of AsPredicted Questions", split_text)
  answers$version <- paste(split_text[version_index], collapse = " ")

  return(answers)
}
```

```{r}
# Initialize empty data frame to store results
all_files_df <- data.frame(
  file_name = character(),
  project_id = character(),
  parent_id = character(),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

osf_ids_vector <- as.character(all_osf_links_df$osf_project_id) # extract the column
osf_ids_vector <- osf_ids_vector[!(is.na(osf_ids_vector) | osf_ids_vector == "NA")]
osf_ids_vector <- unique(osf_ids_vector)                    # remove duplicates

for (i in 1:length(osf_ids_vector)) {
  link <- as.character(osf_ids_vector[i])  # Get the osf_id
  if (is.na(link) || link == "NA" || link == "") {
    print(paste("Skipping row", i, "- link is NA or empty"))
    next
  }
  
  # print("Waiting a second for rate limitations")
  # Sys.sleep(5)
  
  print(link)
  print(i)
  
  # Wrap all risky calls in tryCatch
  result <- tryCatch({
    osf_id <- as_id(link)  # may error if invalid ID
    osf_project <- osf_retrieve_node(osf_id)
    wiki_link <- GET(osf_project[[3]][[1]][["relationships"]][["wikis"]][["links"]][["related"]][["href"]])
    wiki_info <- fromJSON(rawToChar(wiki_link$content))$data$links$download
    wiki_info <- tail(wiki_info, 1) # take last wiki
    wiki <- if (is.null(wiki_info)) NA else content(GET(wiki_info), as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8")
        
    children_resp <- GET(osf_project[[3]][[1]][["relationships"]][["children"]][["links"]][["related"]][["href"]])
    # If GET returns error status, stop to catch below
    if (http_error(children_resp)) {
      stop(paste("HTTP error", status_code(children_resp)))
    }
    children <- fromJSON(rawToChar(children_resp$content))[["data"]][["id"]]
    
    # Combine osf_project$id with children (if not NULL)
    project_ids <- c(osf_project$id, if (!is.null(children)) children)
    
    pid <- project_ids[1]
    
    for (pid in project_ids) {
      tryCatch({
        project_node <- osf_retrieve_node(pid)
        files <- osf_ls_files(project_node)
        title <- osf_project$name
        if (nrow(files) > 0) {
          temp_df <- data.frame(
            file_name = files$name,
            project_id = pid,
            parent_id = osf_project$id,
            folder_name = project_node$name,
            title = title,
            wiki = wiki,
            stringsAsFactors = FALSE
          )
          all_files_df <<- bind_rows(all_files_df, temp_df)  # use <<- to update outside the tryCatch
        }
      }, error = function(e) {
        # Handle 403/404 inside inner loop
        if (grepl("403|404", e$message)) {
          message(paste("Skipping project ID", pid, "- error:", e$message))
        } else {
          stop(e)  # re-throw other errors
        }
      })
    }
    NULL  # return NULL if all successful
  }, error = function(e) {
    # Catch errors from outer calls (like as_id or osf_retrieve_node for link)
    if (grepl("403|404", e$message)) {
      message(paste("Skipping OSF link", link, "- error:", e$message))
      NULL
    } else {
      stop(e)  # re-throw unexpected errors
    }
  })
}

all_files_df
```

```{r}
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(osf_files))) {
      # Read in the R code
      download_link <- osf_files[[3]][[i]][["links"]][["download"]]
      print(download_link)
      
      # Use tryCatch to handle warnings when reading the file
      r_code <- tryCatch(
        readLines(url(download_link)),
        warning = function(w) {
          cat(sprintf("Skipping file due to warning: %s\n", conditionMessage(w)))
          return(NULL)
        },
        error = function(e) {
          cat(sprintf("Skipping file due to error: %s\n", conditionMessage(e)))
          return(NULL)
        }
      )
      
      # Skip further processing if the code is NULL
      if (is.null(r_code)) next

      # Search for absolute file paths (both Windows and Unix)
      absolute_paths <- grep('(["\'])([A-Za-z]:\\\\|/|~)', r_code, value = TRUE)

      # Print the result
      if (length(absolute_paths) > 0) {
        cat("We found the following absolute paths:\n")
        cat(absolute_paths, sep = "\n")
      } else {
        cat("There are no absolute paths, well done!\n")
      }

      # Find lines where libraries are loaded
      library_lines <- grep("\\b(library|require)\\(", r_code)

      # Check if libraries are loaded at multiple places
      if (length(library_lines) > 1 && !all(diff(library_lines) == 1)) {
        cat("Libraries are loaded in multiple places in the script:\n")
        cat(sprintf("Line %d: %s\n", library_lines, r_code[library_lines]), sep = "")
      } else if (length(library_lines) > 0) {
        cat("Libraries are loaded in a single block, well done!\n")
      } else {
        # Warning if no libraries are loaded
        cat("Warning: No libraries are specified in this script.\n")
      }
    }
  }
}
```

## Menial tasks

There is a range of common mistakes that can easily be automatically checked. We will illustrates the usefulness of Papercheck to perform such menial tasks in X examples.

The first example is to identify the presence of anonimized links in the published version of articles. Researchers often want to make their preregistration or files available to reviewers, but links to online repositories would reveal their identity, which is not in line with the blinding a manuscript for peer review. To solve this problem platforms such as the Open Science Framework (OSF) and AsPredicted have created 'view only' or 'blind' links, which allow peer reviewers to gian access to preregistrations and files, without revealing the name of the researchers. Researchers often forget to change these blinded links to the public links. A simple text search is sufficient to find blinded links in manuscripts, and remind authors (or editors) to update these links when checking proofs.

```{r}

RGX_ASPREDICTED <- "aspredicted"
text_found <- search_text(xml, RGX_ASPREDICTED, return = "paragraph")
# blind links often end up having a space in the extracted hyperlink. 
# e.g., https://aspredicted.org/blind.php? x=6uq6sx which should have been extracted as https://aspredicted.org/blind.php?x=6uq6sx
# So we fix it by removing the space. 
text_found$text <- gsub("blind\\.php\\?\\s*", "blind.php?", text_found$text)
RGX_ASPREDICTED_LINK <- "aspredicted\\.org/\\s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{5}"
text_found_as_predicted <- search_text(text_found, RGX_ASPREDICTED_LINK, return = "match")
RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND <- "http://aspredicted\\.org/blind\\.php\\?x=s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{6}"
text_found_as_predicted_blind <- search_text(text_found, RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND, return = "match")

RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND <- "http://aspredicted\\.org/blind\\.php\\?x=s*[a-zA-Z0-9]{6}"
text_found_as_predicted_blind <- search_text(text_found, RGX_ASPREDICTED_BLIND, return = "match")

# Remove duplicates
text_found_as_predicted_blind <- text_found_as_predicted_blind %>% distinct(text, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Define the regular expression pattern for detecting OSF URLs 
RGX_VIEWONLY <- "view_only"
text_found <- search_text(xml, RGX_VIEWONLY, return = "paragraph")
text_found$text <- gsub("/\\? view_only", "/?view_only", text_found$text)

text_found <- text_found %>% distinct(text, .keep_all = TRUE)

```

We find 5 papers which have been published with blind AsPredicted links, and 32 with view only OSF links.

### Check pubpeer comments for references.

We can check pubpeer for comments:

We will just link to the comments, maybe some text summary, but that is it. Optionally, remove statcheck ones.

For example, the DOI https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.657 has a pubpeer comment. It is a statcheck automated test comment, so not interesting. We first encode the DOI in URL format, then turn it into the search command:

```{r}

get_pubpeer_comment <- function(doi) {
  url <- "https://pubpeer.com/v3/publications?devkey=PubPeerZotero"
  
  body <- list(
    dois = list(tolower(doi))
  )
  
  response <- POST(
    url,
    body = toJSON(body, auto_unbox = TRUE),
    encode = "raw",
    add_headers(`Content-Type` = "application/json;charset=UTF-8")
  )
  
  if (status_code(response) == 200) {
    data <- content(response, as = "parsed", type = "application/json")
    if (length(data[["feedbacks"]]) > 0) {
      return(list(
        total_comments = data[["feedbacks"]][[1]][["total_comments"]],
        url = data[["feedbacks"]][[1]][["url"]],
        users = strsplit(data[["feedbacks"]][[1]][["users"]], ",\\s*")[[1]]
      ))
    } else {
      return(NULL)  # No feedback found
    }
  } else {
    return(NULL)  # Request failed
  }
}


get_pubpeer_comment("10.1037/0022-3514.81.4.657")

```

### Work with references

```{r}
get_doi <- function(reference) {
  tryCatch({
    res <- cr_works(query = reference, limit = 1)
    if (nrow(res$data) > 0) {
      return(res$data$doi[1])
    } else {
      return(NA)
    }
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(NA)
  })
}


check_pubpeer_for_references <- function(refs) {
  # Initialize progress bar
  pb <- txtProgressBar(min = 0, max = length(refs), style = 3)
  
  results <- vector("list", length(refs))
  
  for (i in seq_along(refs)) {
    doi <- get_doi(refs[i])
    feedback <- get_pubpeer_comment(doi)
    
    results[[i]] <- list(
      reference = refs[i],
      doi = doi,
      total_comments = if (!is.null(feedback)) feedback$total_comments else NA,
      pubpeer_url = if (!is.null(feedback)) feedback$url else NA,
      users = if (!is.null(feedback)) paste(feedback$users, collapse = ", ") else NA
    )
    
    setTxtProgressBar(pb, i)
  }
  
  close(pb)
  
  # Convert to data frame
  results_df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(results, as.data.frame))
  return(results_df)
}

# Loop over all references

# Initialize an empty list to store results
pubpeer_results <- list()

ids <- names(xml)
total <- length(ids)
i <- 1
for (i in 1:1) {
  id <- ids[i]
  refs <- xml[[id]][["references"]]
  
  if (!is.null(refs) && length(refs) > 0) {
    refs <- refs[!is.na(refs) & nzchar(refs)]  # Clean missing/empty entries
    
    if (length(refs) > 0) {
      cat(sprintf("Checking references for %s (%d/%d) ...\n", id, i, total))
      pubpeer_results[[id]] <- check_pubpeer_for_references(refs)
    } else {
      pubpeer_results[[id]] <- NULL
    }
  } else {
    pubpeer_results[[id]] <- NULL
  }
}

save(pubpeer_results, file = "pubpeerresults_first_447.Rdata")
```

# Discussion

To prevent widespread misuse of an automated tool such as Papercheck, it is important to realize the limits of the tool. Although it might seem desirable to develop modules with high accuracy, a cost-benefit analysis might indicate that at this phase it is more important to invest time to develop 10 modules that assist researchers to check their papers with a relatively high error rate, then to spend the same time on two modules that can be used meta-scientifically with very low error rates. The flexibility of human language combined with the lack of standardization in how researchers report information in scientific manuscripts are such that reducing error rates from 50% to 20% is much easier than reducing error rates from 20% to 5%. Our current approach is to follow the Pareto principle and focus on the 20% of the ways in which researchers get something wrong, that when when identified, would prevent 80% of the times researchers get something wrong.
